caption:
Walmart is giving AI agents their own profiles inside your account so they can shop for you.
You choose: approve every order, or let the agent spend up to a limit you set, like $50 or $100.
Agents never see your card, and agents that break Walmart's rules get blocked. Amazon is blocking shopping agents instead.

Would you let an AI agent buy your groceries?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Walmart

slides.heading: Each agent gets its *own profile*

site_article.headline: Walmart will let AI agents shop for customers within spending limits they set
site_article.dek: The retailer is adding separate agent profiles, a developer gateway built on MCP and a set of rules that agents must follow or be blocked.
site_article.summary: Walmart announced on October 21, 2026, that customers will be able to let AI agents shop for them through dedicated agent profiles, with either approval for every order or a spending limit. A new Agent Gateway for developers is in beta, and agents that break Walmart's terms will be blocked.
site_article.seo_title: Walmart lets AI agents shop for customers with spending limits
site_article.seo_description: Walmart is adding agent profiles, spending limits and an MCP Agent Gateway so AI agents can shop for customers, while Amazon keeps blocking them.
site_article.answer_summary: Yes. Walmart said AI agents will be able to shop for customers through their own profiles inside a Walmart account, either with approval for each purchase or within a spending limit the customer sets. The agents never receive card numbers.
site_article.hero_alt: A robot pushing a shopping cart down a supermarket aisle while looking at a phone.

paragraphs.text: Walmart announced on October 21, 2026, a set of tools that let customers send AI agents to shop for them at Walmart and Sam's Club. The plan has three parts: agent profiles inside a customer's account, a direct connection for developers called the Walmart Agent Gateway, and a list of terms that every agent has to follow.

Today an AI agent that shops at Walmart signs in with the customer's own account, so its purchases look the same as the customer's. Under the new system, each agent a customer authorizes gets a separate profile, and its orders are shown apart from the customer's own. Walmart said Agent Profiles will launch within the next month, which PYMNTS reported as November.

The company compared the setup to adding a cardholder to a credit card account. The agent gets its own way to pay, with limits the customer controls, and the customer can switch it off or delete the profile at any time. A profile is created automatically the first time a customer shops through the gateway from an agent's app.

Customers choose between two modes. In the default mode, the agent needs approval for every purchase. In the other, it can buy on its own up to a spending limit, and Walmart gave $50, $100 and $200 as examples. PPC Land noted that Walmart has not said whether a limit applies per order, per day or per month. Walmart also said it may ask for extra approval even when a purchase is within the limit.

Walmart's terms say agents must not act beyond what the shopper intended, may only reach the information a task needs and the customer allows, and never receive payment card details. Agents cannot add or change payment methods. Walmart's normal return process still applies when an agent does not act as intended, and agents that break the terms will be blocked from the site.

The Agent Gateway is an MCP server, according to Shopifreaks, so agents can search inventory and place orders without browsing the website like a person. Walmart said it can help an agent find a customer's usual items, such as a favorite bread or brand of milk, without handing over the customer's wider shopping history. The gateway is a beta for companies and developers, and PPC Land described it as invitation only. Walmart said agents see the same prices as human shoppers.

The approach contrasts with Amazon. According to PPC Land, Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent from buying on Amazon.com on September 20, 2026, saying it had never agreed to Muse operating in its store and that the agent did not identify itself. Walmart's announcement lists Muse, ChatGPT, Gemini and its own assistant, Sparky, among its existing shopping integrations. PYMNTS reported that Target allows approved agent providers.

Several questions remain open. Walmart has not named the agent companies in the gateway beta, said how it will detect agents that break its terms, or listed which product categories are restricted, PPC Land reported.

By giving agents their own identity and limits, Walmart is treating AI shoppers as a customer channel to manage rather than a bot problem to block. If shoppers adopt agents, that choice could put Walmart in front of the assistants people already use, while Amazon keeps those assistants out of its store.
The next step to watch is the Agent Profiles launch expected in November, and whether Walmart names the agents in its gateway beta and explains how its spending limits work.
